pr_title: Fixed mesh generating convex shapes with duplicate verts.
pr_body: This is to fix https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/41522 where things like flat shaded meshes add the same vertex to the collision shape multiple times for each normal.

issue_context.title: Creating convex collision from a mesh results in duplicate vertices
issue_context.body:
**Godot version:** 3.2.3 RC4

**OS/device including version:** Windows 8.1


**Issue description:** If you go to Mesh|Create Convex Collision Sibling, there are duplicate vertexes in the convex collision shape.  For example, if you create a cube mesh, there will be 24 verts instead of 8.

**Steps to reproduce:**
- Click on a cube mesh.
- Click the mesh menu.
- Create single convex collision sibling
- Look at the collision shape and notice the array size is 24 instead of 8.


**Minimal reproduction project:**
[convex_collision_too_many_verts.zip](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/files/5126790/convex_collision_too_many_verts.zip)


**Note:** I'm working on a fix for this in 3.x, but the code is slightly different in the main branch because pool vectors were removed.  It's just a matter of ignoring verts that are in the same location, because the mesh has duplicate vertices for faces with different normals/uvs/etc.
comments:
Is there any reason against just replacing quickhull with the convex hull algorithm from Bullet?
That one might be more stable?

> Is there any reason against just replacing quickhull with the convex hull algorithm from Bullet?
That one might be more stable?

Bullet may not always be compiled in Godot – in fact, it's planned to move it to a GDNative add-on in the future.

Therefore, we'd need to manually copy Bullet's convex hull algorithm to be able to use it even when Bullet is disabled.

> Therefore, we'd need to manually copy Bullet's convex hull algorithm to be able to use it even when Bullet is disabled.

Is that not an option? Given that our current algorithm seems to be broken in multiple ways?

> Is that not an option? Given that our current algorithm seems to be broken in multiple ways?

It is an option, but adapting Bullet code to use Godot's datatypes may not be trivial.

@Calinou It seems that Bullet's convex hull algorithm is already ported and used in the "vhacd" module, but only used for convex decomposition.
Would it make sense if I adapt it, so it can be used in place of QuickHull?

It is there:
https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/cd05653e308c2263e23debd45211c48af134040d/thirdparty/vhacd/src/btConvexHullComputer.cpp

> Would it make sense if I adapt it, so it can be used in place of QuickHull?

Sure :slightly_smiling_face: 

**Edit:** Pull request opened: https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/47307

Turns out this issue is unrelated to QuickHull.
The collision shape simply stores all the vertices from the source mesh; the convex hull algorithm is only run at a later point in time.
@mortarroad: This doesn't make sense - why use QuickHull at all if the collision shape just skips past it?

QuickHull is only used in the physics server:
https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/3d649d37f8891ff273f5630bb7e9ff842c02f855/servers/physics/shape_sw.cpp#L1152

The resource itself does not apply QuickHull.

It might make sense to run the data through quickhull before storing it so unnecessary verts aren't kept.  The fundamental quickhull algorithm is fine, but there's an issue with the way it tries to maintain edges for display purposes:
1) Unnecessary if only used for collision and the visual is unneeded.
2) Sometimes multiple triangles on the same plane bug it out and create errors: https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/45946

Simply replacing quickhull would mean something else would need to be used for generating the visuals to display the collision.

> Simply replacing quickhull would mean something else would need to be used for generating the visuals to display the collision.

Well, I suppose we would use whatever we replaced QuickHull with... :P 
Like in the PR I made: https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/47307

> 
> 
> > Simply replacing quickhull would mean something else would need to be used for generating the visuals to display the collision.
> 
> Well, I suppose we would use whatever we replaced QuickHull with... :P
> Like in the PR I made: #47307

Ah, cool.  Didn't realize that algorithm saved the edges.  I do have concerns about it possibly being imprecise, though.  Commented in the other thread, but the vhacd algorithm used by the mesh convex_decompose had issues, and I had to switch back to using QuickHull.

Just a note that https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/48533 superceeds the other quickhull replacement.  I imagine it would probably be faster to remove duplicates before running the quickhull algorithm, though.  I can submit a pull request for that (was hesitant to, since the data formats changed for 4.x, but it seems 3.x is still being actively updated).

review_comments:
This loop has O(n²) runtime.
Input meshes may easily have one million or more vertices, which would lead to a very long hang in the editor.

> 
> 
> This loop has O(n²) runtime.
> Input meshes may easily have one million or more vertices, which would lead to a very long hang in the editor.

I would hope somebody isn't trying to use a million+vert mesh as convex collision.  This should just be used for simple shapes.  I think a hang in the editor would be the least of your problems if you tried that.  Do you have a suggestion for an alternative algorithm to check if a vertex already exists before adding it?

I wouldn't even remove the double vertices. That's up to the convex hull algorithm, which should be O(n log n).
I'd say we compute the convex hull right away, or we just leave the data as it is passed in.

But if you really want to remove duplicates, I'd just use a (Hash)set. That works fine if the coordinates are exactly the same.
Efficiently removing doubles with a tolerance is more complicated. I think Blender builds a KD-Tree for that.
The tolerance will only work in one dimension like that. For more dimensions, you need something like a KD tree.

I don't have any references, but I can give you an example.
For this example, let's say the tolerance `DUPLICATE_VERT_EPSILON` is such that two numbers that are an integer are apart are unequal. (e.g. 1 and 2 are different; 1 and 1.9 are equal). E.g. `#define DUPLICATE_VERT_EPSILON 0.99`

Now insert the vectors (0, 0, 0), (-0.9, 1, 0), and (-1.1, 1, 0); in this order. This yields the following tree:
```
             (0, 0, 0)
             /       \
 (-1.1, 1, 0)        (-0.9, 1, 0)
 /          \        /          \
```
(-0.9, 1, 0) is inserted right of (0, 0, 0), because the x compares equal, therefore the y coordinate determines that it is greater.
(-1.1, 1, 0) is inserted left of (0, 0, 0), because -1.1 does not compare equal to 0, and then compares as less, even with the tolerance.

However, (-1.1, 1, 0) and (-0.9, 1, 0) would compare equal; they are only 0.2 apart! But they never get compared with each other.


Yes, the VHACD approach looks interesting.
Sorry, I thought I replied last time. Thanks for your detailed explanation, it makes a lot of sense!
